title: SIGMark: Scalable In-Generation Watermark with Blind Extraction for Video Diffusion
primary_area: alignment, fairness, safety, privacy, and societal considerations

response.summary: SIGMark combines globally reused frame-wise pseudorandom error-correcting codes with a heuristic segment/group recovery procedure to enable metadata-free extraction from diffusion-generated videos. The problem is relevant and the reported HunyuanVideo results are promising, but essential technical details and purported appendices are absent, while the evaluation does not establish reliable detection, security, or broad robustness.
strengths: Addresses a practical scalability limitation of reference-matching in-generation watermarking and presents a clear blind-extraction pipeline (pp. 2–8).
The frame-wise coding and causal-VAE regrouping ideas are sensible, with component ablations showing meaningful gains (Table 3, pp. 9–10).
Evaluates high payloads on 400 generated videos and reports quality, spatial/temporal perturbations, and decoding cost rather than clean bit accuracy alone (pp. 8–10).
weaknesses: The paper repeatedly delegates critical material—distribution-preservation proof, extraction complexity, SGO algorithms, Wan-2.2 results, and PRC robustness—to Appendices A–E, but no appendices are included in the supplied 14 pages (pp. 6–10). This prevents verification and leaves the claimed two-model evaluation unsupported.

Evidence is incomplete for a watermarking system: there are no false-positive/detection results on unmarked videos, message-level recovery rates, uncertainty estimates, adaptive attacks, key-reuse/security analysis, or comparisons with alternative indexed/metadata-free designs. The scalability experiment reaches only 3,200 videos and compares against one baseline (p. 10).

Robustness is tested using a narrow set of synthetic perturbations, with temporal attacks fixed at 30 frames; SIGMark still loses up to 0.14 accuracy spatially and about 0.10 temporally, contrary to the characterization as negligible loss (Table 2, p. 9). SGO also relies on underspecified optical-flow thresholds and padding behavior that may fail on natural cuts or difficult motion (p. 7).
response.score_rationale: The work has a useful problem formulation and a potentially practical combination of PRC coding and temporal regrouping, but its novelty appears mainly compositional and the supplied manuscript omits the appendices needed to validate central claims. Missing detection/security evaluation and limited robustness evidence are substantial for watermarking, placing it below the acceptance threshold despite promising empirical results.

response.summary: SIGMark combines global frame-wise pseudorandom coding with a segment/group-ordering procedure to enable metadata-free extraction and improve robustness to temporal edits in causal-3D-VAE video diffusion models. The direction is practically relevant and results are promising, but central technical, security, and reproducibility claims are insufficiently supported in the supplied manuscript.
strengths: Addresses a meaningful deployment limitation of prior in-generation video watermarks: per-generation metadata and linear template matching; the proposed global-key construction has constant cost with respect to the number of generated videos (pp. 5–6, 10).
The SGO design is tailored to causal temporal compression and combines optical-flow segmentation with PRC-based group-position detection in a plausible way (pp. 6–7).

Experiments cover high-capacity messages, spatial and temporal perturbations, component ablations, and measured decoding-time scaling; SIGMark substantially improves over VideoMark and remains reasonably competitive with VideoShield (pp. 8–10).
weaknesses: Many decisive details are deferred to Appendices A–E—including the distortion-free proof, PRC behavior, extraction complexity, SGO algorithm, and Wan-2.2 results—but no appendices are present in the supplied 14 pages (pp. 6–10). This prevents verification and contradicts the claimed comprehensive two-model evaluation.

The security and detection formulation is incomplete: there is no threat model, false-positive/false-attribution analysis on unwatermarked or adversarial videos, key-compromise discussion, or statistical decoding threshold. Bit accuracy alone does not establish reliable watermark detection or tracing (pp. 4, 8–9).

Evidence for robustness and quality is limited: only one model/task is shown for disturbances and ablations, temporal attacks use one fixed severity, claimed swapping robustness is not evaluated, and no uncertainty or significance is reported. The exact Gaussian/distortion-free claim also relies on unshown assumptions about randomized PRC signs (pp. 6, 8–10).
response.score_rationale: The paper offers a useful, moderately novel systems idea and encouraging empirical results, but the missing appendices and absence of security/detection validation leave core soundness claims unverifiable. The work is near the acceptance boundary but currently falls slightly below it.

response.summary: SIGMark combines globally reused frame-wise pseudorandom codes with temporal regrouping before diffusion inversion, aiming for blind, constant-metadata extraction from generated videos. The direction is useful and results are promising, but the supplied manuscript does not adequately substantiate its robustness, security, or claimed generality.
strengths: Addresses a practical scalability limitation of template-matching in-generation watermarks with a conceptually simple blind extraction design (pp. 4–8).
The causal-VAE grouping failure is clearly motivated, and SGO directly targets frame insertion, deletion, and clipping (pp. 6–7).
Evaluation includes high payloads, 400 generated videos, quality measurements, temporal/spatial perturbations, and component ablations (pp. 8–10).
weaknesses: Key technical details and promised evidence are absent: the manuscript repeatedly refers to Appendices A–E for distribution proofs, algorithms, Wan-2.2 results, prompts, costs, and PRC robustness, but the supplied paper ends with references and contains no appendices (pp. 6–9, 14). This prevents verification and substantially weakens reproducibility.

The robustness claims are overstated. In Table 2, SIGMark loses 0.10 accuracy under frame dropping, comparable to VideoShield's 0.10 loss; VideoShield is also stronger under all tested spatial perturbations. Results lack uncertainty, attack-strength sweeps, adaptive attacks, false-positive analysis, and main-text evidence on Wan-2.2 (pp. 9–10).

Using a global reusable secret-key set creates unexamined security and deployment risks, including key compromise and chosen-sample/adaptive attacks. The scalability experiment reaches only 3,200 stored videos, compares primarily against a linear-scan implementation, and SIGMark itself costs about 14 seconds per video, so “minimal overhead” and million-scale practicality are not established (p. 10).
response.score_rationale: The paper offers a moderately novel and practically motivated combination of PRC-based blind decoding and causal-frame regrouping. However, missing referenced appendices, incomplete cross-model evidence, lack of statistical/security evaluation, and overclaimed robustness leave the technical case marginally below the acceptance bar.

response.summary: SIGMark combines globally shared frame-wise pseudorandom codes with a segment/group recovery procedure to enable metadata-free extraction from diffusion-generated videos. The problem is relevant and the results are promising, but central claims about robustness, distortion-free operation, security, and generality are not supported rigorously enough in the supplied manuscript.
strengths: Addresses a practical limitation of prior inversion-based video watermarks: extraction cost that grows with the reference database; the measured decoding cost remains approximately constant as the database grows (p. 10, Fig. 5).

The frame-wise coding and causal-VAE-aware regrouping form a coherent approach, with ablations indicating that GF-PRC, optical-flow segmentation, and sliding-window detection each contribute (pp. 6–7, 9–10, Table 3).
Experiments cover both high payloads and substantial spatial/temporal disturbances; SIGMark is competitive with non-blind baselines while avoiding sample-specific metadata (pp. 8–9, Tables 1–2).
weaknesses: The evidence is incomplete and sometimes overstated: only HunyuanVideo results appear in the supplied paper despite repeated claims of Wan-2.2 evaluation, and all promised appendices containing proofs, algorithm details, extra results, and robustness analysis are absent (pp. 6–10). The evaluation uses only 400 generated videos and reports no variability or significance (p. 8).

Key watermarking criteria are missing: there is no false-positive/detection analysis on unmarked or unrelated real videos, no adversarial removal/forgery or global-key compromise analysis, and no study of collusion or repeated global-key exposure. Sharing one global key set across all requests may create serious security risks (pp. 5–6, 10).

The robustness and scalability comparisons are narrow. Temporal tests use only random insertion/drop/clipping, while SGO relies on heuristic optical-flow thresholds whose details are absent; reported losses can reach 0.10–0.14 despite being described as negligible (p. 9, Table 2). The scalability baseline assumes exhaustive matching, without examining indexing or alternative blind baselines (p. 10).
response.score_rationale: The paper offers a useful and reasonably novel systems-level combination, and its initial results support feasibility. However, missing appendices and cross-model results, lack of detection/security evaluation, and limited robustness and scalability controls leave important claims insufficiently substantiated. I therefore place it marginally below acceptance, with some uncertainty because material explicitly referenced as appendices was not supplied.

response.summary: SIGMark combines globally reused frame-wise pseudorandom codes with a segment/group-reordering procedure to enable blind extraction of messages embedded in diffusion initial noise. The problem is relevant and the proposed system is promising, but the supplied manuscript does not substantiate several central correctness, security, and scalability claims sufficiently.
strengths: The paper identifies practically important limitations of inversion-based video watermarks—per-sample reference matching and sensitivity to causal-VAE frame grouping—and proposes a coherent end-to-end solution (pp. 2–7).

Evaluation covers T2V and I2V settings, high nominal payloads, spatial/temporal perturbations, and component ablations; the reported results show useful accuracy and clear gains from GF-PRC and SGO (pp. 8–10).
The constant-size key state and roughly constant measured decoding time are attractive for platform deployment relative to the implemented non-blind baseline (p. 10).
weaknesses: Essential material repeatedly cited as Appendices A–E—including the losslessness proof, PRC details, extraction complexity, SGO algorithm, additional Wan-2.2 results, and robustness analysis—is absent from the supplied 14 pages (pp. 6–10). Consequently, core claims cannot be independently checked.

The evidence is incomplete for a security watermark: there are no false-positive/detection results on unwatermarked or out-of-distribution videos, no key-reuse or adaptive-removal/forgery analysis, and SGO lacks specified thresholds and failure behavior. Robustness uses only vaguely parameterized perturbations and random temporal edits (pp. 7–9).

The main quantitative support is limited: only Hunyuan results are shown, uncertainty/significance is absent, and 0.885 bit accuracy at 8192 bits implies many erroneous bits without an exact-message recovery analysis. The scalability comparison also establishes linear cost only for the authors’ baseline implementation, not an unavoidable lower bound for competing indexing or retrieval designs (pp. 8–10).
response.score_rationale: The global-key blind formulation and causal-group recovery idea are useful and moderately novel, with encouraging preliminary results. However, missing appendices and absent security, false-positive, exact-message, and statistically supported evaluations leave the central technical and practical claims under-validated. I therefore rate it below the acceptance threshold, with some uncertainty because the omitted appendices might address several concerns.
